files.lesson.md: --- order: 14 unit: volume node: AC9M8M02 n1 title: Volume and capacity summary: "Volume measures space in cubic units; capacity measures how much a container holds. 1 cm³ holds 1 mL, 1000 cm³ holds 1 L, and 1 m³ holds 1000 L. A cubic metre is 100 × 100 × 100 = 1 000 000 cm³, not 100." language: maths voice: { name: af_heart, speed: 1.1 } hook: "How much water does a box hold, and how do you get it from the box's size? A cubic metre of water weighs about a tonne, but how do litres and cubic centimetres fit together?" connection: rainwater-tank # data/connections/maths.yml app: command: node "$REPO_ROOT/tools/serve.mjs" "$REPO_ROOT/dist/_playground-board" 8305 url: http://127.0.0.1:8305/index.html readySelector: "#gsum" layout: full explainPicture: { ref: prism.yml#explain-pic, caption: "A 10 cm cube: 10 × 10 × 10 = 1000 cm³, which holds exactly 1 L." } explainClip: query: { code: "@prism.yml#explain", fresh: 1, id: explain } caption: "A litre is a 10 cm cube" say: "Fill a ten centimetre cube, layer by layer." clip: - caption: { text: "A 10 cm by 10 cm base: each layer is 100 cm³, so 100 mL.", say: "Each layer is one hundred cubic centimetres: one hundred millilitres." } - wait: 1000 - caption: { text: "Ten layers make 1000 cm³: exactly 1 litre.", say: "Ten layers make one thousand: exactly one litre." } - click: Make the height bigger - click: Make the height bigger - click: Make the height bigger - click: Make the height bigger - click: Make the height bigger - click: Make the height bigger - click: Make the height bigger - click: Make the height bigger - expect: { selector: "#gsum", contains: "1 L" } - wait: 1500 --- **Volume** is the space a solid takes up, in cubic units (cm³, m³). **Capacity** is how much a container holds, in millilitres (mL), litres (L) or kilolitres (kL). How do the two fit together? ## Predict: a 10 cm cube ```step stage: predict insight: "Committing to how much a 10 cm cube holds shows whether they link cm³ to mL, and the size of a litre." check: type: predict q: "A box is 10 cm by 10 cm by 10 cm. How much water does it hold?" options: ["1 L", "100 mL", "10 L", "1000 L"] actual: "1 L. 10 × 10 × 10 = 1000 cm³, and each cm³ holds 1 mL: 1000 mL = 1 L." ``` How many cubic centimetres is it, and how many millilitres is that? ## Run: fill a box ```step stage: run insight: "Building boxes and reading their volume and capacity side by side shows cm³ and mL are the same number." try: { playground: board, starter: "prism.yml#run", height: 600 } check: { type: board, text: "Make a box that holds exactly 1 L. Was your prediction right? Could a box with different lengths also hold 1 L?", when: "v = 1000", explain: "10 × 10 × 10 = 1000 cm³. A 5 × 10 × 20 box (too long for this board) would hold 1 L too: any box of 1000 cm³ does." } ``` The panel gives the volume and the capacity together. Here's how volume and capacity line up. They link exactly: | Volume | Capacity | |---|---| | 1 cm³ | 1 mL | | 1000 cm³ (a 10 cm cube) | 1 L | | 1 m³ | 1000 L = 1 kL | A cubic metre is 100 cm × 100 cm × 100 cm = **1 000 000 cm³**: a length conversion is used three times, once for each direction. Water links the units to mass too. A litre of water has a mass of about a kilogram, so a cubic metre of water, 1000 L, is about a tonne. (That is how the litre was first defined: from 1901 to 1964 it was "the volume occupied by a mass of 1 kilogram of pure water" at its greatest density, [BIPM, 1901](https://www.bipm.org/committees/cg/cgpm/3-1901/resolution-1).) ## Investigate: converting units ```step stage: investigate insight: "1 m³ = 1000 L; converting cubic units uses the length factor three times (Ravi uses it once); the unit should suit the context." tasks: - check: type: number q: "How many litres does 1 m³ hold?" answer: 1000 tolerance: 0 explain: "1 m³ = 100 × 100 × 100 = 1 000 000 cm³ = 1 000 000 mL = 1000 L." - check: type: bug code: "working.txt#ravi" text: "Ravi works out how much a 2 m³ tank holds. Click the line where his working goes wrong." answer: 2 fault: logic misconception: cube-conversion explain: "Line 2: a cubic metre is 100 cm in each of three directions: 100 × 100 × 100 = 1 000 000 cm³. The tank holds 2000 L." - check: type: question q: "Which unit suits the capacity of a backyard swimming pool?" options: ["Kilolitres (or cubic metres)", "Millilitres", "Cubic centimetres", "Litres, to the nearest millilitre"] answer: 0 feedback: [null, "Millions of them: far too small a unit.", "Tens of millions: far too small.", "A pool cannot be measured that precisely."] explain: "A backyard pool might hold something like 30 kilolitres (30 cubic metres), a size made up for the task." ``` ### Cubic metres ### Find the mistake Read Ravi's working. How many cm are in each direction of a cubic metre? ### Choosing units ## Modify: tanks and cartons ```step stage: modify insight: "Building a tank in metres, converting both ways, and the difference between cm and cm³." try: { playground: board, starter: "prism.yml#tank", height: 600 } tasks: - starter: "prism.yml#tank" hint: ["24 000 L is 24 m³.", "Try a base of 4 m by 3 m."] check: { type: board, text: "Make a water tank that holds 24 000 L.", when: "c = 24000", explain: "24 000 L = 24 m³: for example 4 m × 3 m × 2 m." } - check: type: number q: "A jug holds 2.5 L. How many cm³ is that?" answer: 2500 tolerance: 0 explain: "1 L = 1000 cm³, so 2.5 L = 2500 cm³." - check: type: number q: "A cup holds 350 mL. How many cm³ is that?" answer: 350 tolerance: 0 explain: "1 mL = 1 cm³, so 350 cm³." - check: type: question q: "Which of these is a volume?" options: ["12 cm³", "12 cm", "12 cm²", "12 kg"] answer: 0 feedback: [null, "A length.", "An area.", "A mass."] explain: "Volume is in cubic units: cm³." ``` ### A tank ### Litres to cm³ ### Millilitres to cm³ ### Which is a volume? ## Practise: volume and capacity ```step stage: practise insight: "Conversions both ways and a box's capacity, mixed; using 100 instead of 1 000 000 for m³ is the planted slip; the triangular prism review keeps base times height fresh." tasks: - check: type: number q: "Write 4500 mL in litres." answer: 4.5 tolerance: 0 explain: "4500 ÷ 1000 = 4.5 L." - check: type: number q: "A container holds 0.6 m³. How many litres is that?" answer: 600 tolerance: 0 explain: "0.6 × 1000 = 600 L." smaller: check: { type: number, q: "A cubic metre is 100 cm long, 100 cm wide and 100 cm high. How many cm³ is that?", answer: 1000000, tolerance: 0, explain: "100 × 100 × 100 = 1 000 000 cm³, and a litre is 1000 of them. So how many litres in one cubic metre?" } - check: type: number q: "A box is 20 cm by 15 cm by 10 cm. How many litres does it hold?" answer: 3 tolerance: 0 explain: "20 × 15 × 10 = 3000 cm³ = 3000 mL = 3 L." - check: type: number q: "Review: a triangular prism has a right-triangle end with legs 3 cm and 4 cm, and is 10 cm long. What is its volume in cm³?" answer: 60 tolerance: 0 explain: "Base area ½ × 3 × 4 = 6 cm², times 10 = 60 cm³." ``` ### mL to L ### m³ to L ### A box ### Review: triangular prisms ## Make: a juice carton ```step stage: make insight: "Designing to a capacity with a constraint uses volume and capacity together." try: { playground: board, starter: "prism.yml#carton", height: 600 } hint: ["600 mL = 600 cm³.", "Try a base of 10 cm by 6 cm."] check: { type: board, text: "Design a carton that holds 600 mL, with a base that is not square (l more than w).", when: "c = 600 and l > w", explain: "For example 10 × 6 × 10, or 12 × 5 × 10." } ``` Then say which of your designs would fit best in a lunch box, and why. ## Make: a tank for the roof, on paper ```step stage: make insight: "Rain on a roof is a thin layer: 1 mm over 1 m² is 0.001 m³, which is 1 L. The tank's volume in m³ then becomes litres, and the two are compared." hint: ["Find the rain in litres, then the tank in litres.", "1 mm of rain on 1 m² is 1 L; 1 m³ holds 1000 L."] check: type: reasoning paper: true q: "A roof has an area of 80 m². In a storm 30 mm of rain falls on it, and all of it runs into an empty tank that is 1.5 m long, 1 m wide and 1.2 m high. By how many litres does the rain overflow the tank?" steps: - ["$80 \\times 30 = 2400$ L of rain", "1 mm of rain on 1 m² is 1 L"] - ["Tank: $1.5 \\times 1 \\times 1.2 = 1.8$ m³, and $1.8 \\times 1000 = 1800$ L", "1 m³ holds 1000 L"] - ["$2400 - 1800 = 600$ L", "rain minus what the tank holds"] picks: - step: 1 q: "Why does 1 mm of rain on 1 m² make 1 L?" options: - "A layer 1 mm deep over 1 m² is 0.001 m³, and 0.001 m³ is 1 L" - "1 mm is the same as 1 mL" - "A litre is defined as a square metre of rain" answer: 0 feedback: [null, "1 mm is a length and 1 mL is a volume. It is the layer's volume, 1 m² × 0.001 m, that equals 1 L.", "A litre is 1000 cm³. Rain over 1 m², 1 mm deep, happens to be exactly that."] answer: "600" tolerance: 0 feedback: - ["1800", "That is how much the tank holds. The question asks how much is left over."] - ["2400", "That is all the rain. Take away what the tank holds."] - ["0.6", "That is in cubic metres. The question asks for litres."] criteria: - "I changed rain on the roof into litres, and the tank into litres." - "I changed m³ to litres by multiplying by 1000." - "I took the tank's capacity away from the rain." explain: "Rain: 80 × 30 = 2400 L. Tank: 1.5 × 1 × 1.2 = 1.8 m³ = 1800 L. The overflow is 2400 − 1800 = 600 L. The Bureau of Meteorology calls the 1 mm = 1 L rule approximate, and real tanks collect less than falls on the roof." ``` Do this one in your book, not on the screen. The roof, the storm and the tank are made up for the task. Write the rain and the tank in litres, then type the overflow. **Also used in** - **Rainwater tanks.** The Bureau of Meteorology says 1 mm of rain on 1 m² gives about 1 L, an approximation ([Bureau of Meteorology](https://www.bom.gov.au/climate/how/faq-data.shtml)). Real tanks collect less, because some water is lost. - **Pool dosing.** The label is per 10 000 L, so the pool's volume in m³ is changed to litres first. - **Cartons.** A 1 L carton holds 1000 cm³, about a 10 cm cube. ```teacher summary: Students build boxes and tanks, read their volume and capacity together, and convert between cm³, mL, L and m³ (AC9M8M02, node 1). time: 35 timing: Predict and Run 8 min · Investigate 8 min · Modify 10 min · Practise and Make 9 min goals: - I can convert between cm³, mL, L and m³. - I can explain why 1 m³ is 1 000 000 cm³. - I can choose a sensible unit for a container. struggle: Converting cubic units. Ask students to draw a cube and label 100 cm on all three edges before they convert. before: > Do the Run board yourself first. Bring a 1 L carton and a 10 cm cube (or a drawing) if you can. The one idea: 1 cm³ holds 1 mL, so 1000 cm³ is 1 L, and 1 m³ (100 × 100 × 100 cm³) is 1000 L. The common mistake is converting a cubic unit with the length factor once (Ravi's mistake). The board gives capacity in mL or L for cm and in L for m. Wider: why a cubic metre of water has a mass of about a tonne, and water storage in kilolitres or megalitres (dams, town water). running: - "Predict: ask students to show the size of a litre with their hands." - "Run: ask for two different boxes that hold 1 L." - "Investigate: ask Ravi to draw his cubic metre." - "Modify: ask which unit a council would use for a dam." - "Make: ask whose carton is easiest to hold." - "Paper: the rainwater tank is worked in books. Books out; look for both amounts in litres before they are compared, and ask why 1 mm on 1 m² is 1 L." stuck: - see: A student says 1 m³ = 100 cm³. ask: How many cm along each of the three edges? fix: 100 × 100 × 100 = 1 000 000 cm³. - see: A student mixes up cm and cm³. ask: Is that a length, an area or a volume? fix: Cubic units for volume. - see: A student divides by 100 for mL to L. ask: How many mL in a litre? fix: 1000 mL = 1 L. stretch: A rainwater tank is 2 m long, 2 m wide and 1.5 m tall. How many days would it supply a family that uses 180 L a day? support: Keep the conversion table visible; use real containers labelled in mL and L. leads: > This starts AC9M8M02. Where it leads: prism problems (next lesson), and volume of cylinders (Year 9). exit: q: A fish tank is 50 cm by 30 cm by 40 cm. How many litres does it hold? a: 50 × 30 × 40 = 60 000 cm³ = 60 L. explain: > **Volume** is in cubic units; **capacity** is in mL, L or kL. 1 cm³ holds 1 mL, 1000 cm³ holds 1 L, and 1 m³ holds 1000 L. A cubic metre is 100 cm × 100 cm × 100 cm = 1 000 000 cm³: convert each of the three lengths. ```

files.working.txt:
# Ravi's working for the "find the mistake" task. Plain text: students click the wrong line, nothing runs.

# region: ravi
A water tank holds 2 m³.
1 m = 100 cm, so 1 m³ = 100 cm³.
So the tank holds 2 × 100 = 200 cm³.
That is 200 mL.
# endregion
